background_notes.fact: For every real s, spatial reflection with sign Jf(x)=-f(-x) is an isometric involution on the mean-zero homogeneous and inhomogeneous Fourier Sobolev spaces, preserving reality. The multipliers S_t and the source untwisting multipliers exp(-it k^3) are strongly continuous isometries on these spaces. Thus a continuous twisted H^s path untwists to a continuous physical H^s path; J and these multipliers preserve convergence used in smooth approximation.

grounds.reason: The Fourier normalization specifies the reflection coefficient identity.
H^s is defined by the weighted square sum and reality by coefficient conjugacy.
The homogeneous norms are on the mean-zero subspace.

background_notes.justification: Change variables x to -x modulo 2pi to obtain (Jf)^hat(k)=-f^hat(-k), first for polynomials and then by completion. The weights are even, which proves the isometry and real/mean-zero assertions. Multiplier continuity follows by approximating a fixed vector by a finite Fourier sum: its finite part is continuous in t and the remaining weighted square norm stays uniformly small by isometry. For a varying path split the difference into the path difference and the multiplier difference on a fixed vector. Apply these bounded maps to each approximating path; the same split proves continuity and preserves convergence.

background_notes.fact: For U in C([0,T];L^2(Torus)), the distributional source equation U_t=UU_x+U_xxx, with UU_x=(1/2)partial_x(U^2), is equivalent to the coefficient integral equation stated in E001 for z_k(t)=exp(ik^3t) U^hat(t)(k). Such z is in L^infinity([0,T];dot H^0) when U is mean-zero. Reflection J transports this equation to u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2). Hence continuous L^2 solutions lie in the stated source uniqueness class after inverse reflection.

background_notes.justification: For each k, the convolution sum of U^hat(l)U^hat(k-l) converges absolutely by Cauchy-Schwarz and is the kth coefficient of U^2. This follows first for Fourier polynomials and then from their L^2 convergence, since ||f^2-g^2||_1 <= (||f||_2+||g||_2)||f-g||_2. Thus each nonlinear Fourier coefficient is continuous in time. Fourier testing gives d U^hat(k)/dt=-ik^3 U^hat(k)+(ik/2)sum_l U^hat(l)U^hat(k-l); multiplying by exp(ik^3t) and integrating yields exactly the phase exp(i3k l(k-l)t). Conversely these integrated identities imply the distributional equation, first for finite spatial Fourier tests and then for smooth tests by their Fourier convergence and the L^2/L^1 bounds. A continuous L^2 path is bounded on the compact time interval, and twisting preserves its norm. Reflection is a continuous change of variables on distributions, with the derivative signs computed in S002, so the same identities apply to the limiting solution and to any competing continuous L^2 solution.

background_notes.fact: If every finite weighted Fourier square sum of a mean-zero path is at most C^2, with C>=0, its full homogeneous H^gamma norm is at most C. These finite-sum inequalities pass through coefficientwise convergence. An a.e.-in-time uniform Sobolev bound on a continuous Sobolev path extends to every time.

background_notes.justification: For each finite cutoff, coefficient convergence gives convergence of the finite sum. The full nonnegative series is the supremum over these increasing finite sums, so a common squared-norm upper bound persists. If a continuous norm exceeded its essential upper bound at any time, continuity would give a nonempty relative time interval of positive measure where it also exceeded that bound, a contradiction. Here E001 already gives the limiting bound; the finite-sum reasoning only explains the stated passage to it and introduces no additional compactness claim.

background_notes.fact: A smooth periodic datum has finite H^m and dot H^m norms for every positive integer m. A periodic KdV path belonging to C([0,T];H^m) for every such m is smooth in space and time (with one-sided time derivatives at the endpoints). The smooth-path twist v=S_(-t)u is differentiable and satisfies v'=(1/2)B_t(v,v).

background_notes.justification: Repeated integration by parts gives arbitrarily fast Fourier decay for smooth data. For a path in all H^m, Cauchy-Schwarz with m>j+1/2 gives absolute, uniformly convergent Fourier series for each jth spatial derivative; continuity in H^m gives joint continuity. Products are continuous in each integer H^m for m>=1: by the Leibniz rule, in every derivative term up to order m, one factor has derivative order at most m-1 and is bounded by its H^1 norm via the same Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz estimate, while the other is in L^2. The distributional equation consequently has a continuous right side in any desired H^r, using continuity of u in a sufficiently higher H^m. Integrating it in H^r gives a continuously differentiable time path there. Repeating this argument with the differentiated polynomial equation yields every time derivative and joint smoothness. Finally differentiating S_(-t) on these smooth paths gives v'=S_(-t)(u_t+u_xxx)=S_(-t)partial_x(u^2)/2=B_t(v,v)/2, exactly the identity in S002.
